entries.modern_form: PIE *h₂ep- 'water, body of water; river' (Pokorny 2. ap- 51, with the by-form ab- 1); Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hā́ps > Proto-Iranian *Hā́fš
entries.note: Pokorny IEW p.1 has 'ab- Wasser, Fluß' (Lat. amnis, OIr. ab, Welsh afon) and refers to '2. ap- Wasser, Fluß' on p.51 (Skt. ap-, Av. āfš/āpəm, Hitt. ḫap(a)-, Toch. āp); Nourai's double heading 'Ab 1, Ap 1' merely combines the two Pokorny lemmas, which modern scholarship (Wiktionary after Wodtko-Irslinger-Schneider NIL, Rastorgueva-Edelman ESIJa I 312) treats as variants of one root *h₂ep-/*h₂eb-. AHD/Watkins: 'ap-2 Water, river. Iranian ap- in Persian ab, water: JULEP [Pok. 2. ap- 51]'. Root, language label and gloss are correct. Weak points on this page are the four sub-derivations in node 2 (āftāb, ābādān, āxwarr are NOT from āb 'water' in modern etymology), the whole ābnīk > al-anbīq > alembic branch (nodes 5-6; every modern source derives anbīq from Greek ámbix, as Nourai's own NOTE half-admits), and the 'Sanskrit' label on Punjab (node 15), which is a Persian coinage.

ref_check.note: POK_01.txt line 19 (IEW p.1): 'ab- Wasser, Fluß. Lat. amnis ... air. ab ... cymr. afon ... Vgl. auch 2. ap- Wasser, Fluß und abō(n) Affe'. The Iranian forms are under 2. ap- p.51 (English edition POK_full.txt: 'Root ap-2 (*hap-2) water, river ... Old Indic ap- f. water ... Avestan Nom. Sg. āfš, Akk. Sg. āpəm'). Pokorny is still the standard reference for this root.

nodes.derivation: Avestan āp- f. 'water' (nom. sg. āfš, acc. āpəm, gen. pl. apąm, cf. the month-name Ābān 'of the waters'), Old Persian ap- (loc. sg. apiyā in DSf) both continue Proto-Iranian *Hā́fš < PIIr. *Hā́ps < PIE *h₂ep- (Skt. āp-, pl. āpaḥ; Hitt. ḫap(a)- 'river'; Lat. amnis < *abnis). In Middle Persian the word is āp/āb (Book Pahlavi ʾp, Manichaean ʾb; MacKenzie 'ab ... water'), the intervocalic/final -p- lenited to -b (spirant β) in the Sasanian period. The label 'Avestan / Pahlavi' correctly collapses the Old-Iranian and Middle-Persian stages.

ref_check.note: KLN_1966.txt line 1142 (p.2, s.v. abdest): 'Pers. āb, water, is rel. to Avestic āp-, OI. āpaḥ (fem. pl.), water; see amnic and cp. the first element in abkari and the second element in doab and in julep.'

nodes.derivation: Only one of the four compounds really contains āp 'water'. (a) âp-tab = MP āftāb 'sunshine, sun' (Pahlavi ʾptʾb; NP āftāb): modern etymology (Cheung 2007 s.v. tap; Wiktionary) derives it from Proto-Iranian *abi-tāpah 'shining upon', i.e. the preverb abi- (> MP af-/āf-) + tāp- 'to shine, be hot'; Horn (Grundriss no. 3) likewise separated an āb 'Glanz' (cf. Skt. ābhā-) from āb 'water'. Nourai's gloss 'a (hot) glittering object' shows he is forcing āb 'water/lustre' into the compound; the water-root is not involved. (b) zâ-âp = MP zahābag (MacKenzie: 'zahabag [zhʾpk, NP zahāb] spring, source') = *zah 'spring, depth' + āb + suffix -ag; this one is genuinely āb 'water' and gives NP zahāb/zāb. (c) ô-pât-ân = ābādān: as a common noun MP ābādān 'thriving, populous' is ā-pāta- 'protected, cultivated' (root pā- 'protect', Nourai's own ☞Pa) + -ān, with no water element; as the city name, medieval Arabic ʿAbbādān (Balādhurī: founded by ʿAbbād of Tamīm; Ptolemy/Marcian Apphadana/Apphana) was officially respelled Ābādān in 1935, and the 'āb + pā(d) coast-guard station' reading is a modern proposal by B. Farahvashi (= Nourai's IRN), not a demonstrated etymology. (d) av-xur = MP āxwarr 'manger, stable' (Pahlavi ʾhwl; NP āxor/āxur, Arm. axoṙ): MacKenzie and Wiktionary derive it from ā- + xwar- 'eat' (Proto-Iranian *hwar-), literally 'eating-place'; the first element is the preverb ā-, not āb 'water', so the 'drinking' sense is a folk etymology.

Farahvashi proposed derivation from Persian ab (water) + pā (guard, watch), i.e. coastguard station', so the reference presumably says what the arrow says; it is a hypothesis not adopted by Iranica.
Khaleqi Motlaq, Asās-e Eshteqāq-e Fārsi — no online copy.

MacKenzie (PHD_mackenzie.txt line 658 'ab [MYA ...] water'; 5730 'zahabag [zhʾpk, N zahāb] spring, source'; 12387 axwarr) — supports zahāb, but lists āxwarr and ābād(ān) 'populous, thriving, prosperous' as separate lemmas, not compounds of ab. (Not cited by Nourai for this node; checked as the modern standard.)

nodes.derivation: NP āb 'water' is the direct continuation of MP āb/āp (< OP ap-, Av. āp-); the MP final spirant β became NP b. zahāb (also zāb, and the river-name Zāb) 'spring, seepage water' continues MP zahābag 'spring, source' (MacKenzie), i.e. zah 'spring, depth' (Wiktionary زه, Etymology 3: 'from Middle Persian *zah, attested in zahābag') + āb; the MP suffix -ag was dropped as usual in NP. Mo'in defines zahāb as 'a seepage point near a spring or watercourse where thin streams of water emerge'. Of the extra words: ābān (month, Av. apąm 'of the waters'), gulāb, ābšār, āsyāb (MacKenzie asyab '(water-)mill') are genuine āb-compounds; ābādān and āxor/āxur are not (see node 2).

nodes.derivation: English julep (late 14th c., 'syrupy drink in which medicine is given') < Old French julep < Medieval Latin julapium < Arabic julāb < Persian gulāb 'rose-water' = gul 'rose' (Nourai's ☞Wrdho, OIr. *wr̥da-) + āb 'water'. Arabic replaced the non-Arabic g by j and Latin/Romance supplied the -ep/-apium ending; the 'mint julep' sense is American, 1761. The chart's direct Persian → English arrow skips the Arabic, Latin and French intermediaries but the ultimate source is right (AHD, Klein, Etymonline all agree).

ref_check.note: AHD_watkins1985.txt line 282 'ap-2 ... Persian ab, water: JULEP' and line 1174 'Zero-grade form *wrd- in Iranian *wrd in Persian gul, rose: JULEP'; index line 1707 'JULEP ap-2, wrod-'. Klein p.2 s.v. abdest and p.836 s.v. julep ('fr. Pers. gulāb, rose water, julep, compounded of gul, rose, and āb, water') agree.

nodes.derivation: Nourai analyses the Arabic al-anbīq 'still' as a Persian compound āb 'water' + nīk 'good' (☞Nei 1), i.e. 'good (distilled) water', following Asbaghi (PLA). No Persian dictionary knows āb-nīk as a common noun: vajehyab returns only Dehkhoda's 'آب نیک: نام قریه‌ای از رودبار در ایالت طهران' (a village name), and Mo'in labels انبیق itself '[غ. معر.]' = Greek, arabicized. All modern etymological sources (Klein, Etymonline, Wiktionary, Beekes) derive Arabic إنبيق from Greek ἄμβιξ 'spouted cup, cap of a still' (Syriac ʾambīqā as intermediary); the initial a-/in- of anbīq/inbīq reflects Greek am-/Syriac am- with nasal dissimilation, not Persian āb. The 'âbnîk' etymon is therefore a folk-etymological back-formation and the node should be rejected.

ref_check.note: Asbaghi, Persische Lehnwörter im Arabischen — no online copy. Mo'in (MON_part1.txt line 17169) contradicts: 'انبیق: [غ. معر.] (ا.) ظرفی است برای تقطیر مایعات و گرفتن عصاره و عرق' — marked as Greek, arabicized.

nodes.derivation: Arabic إِنْبِيق inbīq / أَنْبِيق anbīq (with article al-anbīq) 'distilling apparatus' is a borrowing of Greek ἄμβιξ (gen. ἄμβικος) 'spouted cup; cap of a still', a word already used by the Alexandrian alchemists (Zosimus, 3rd-4th c.); it reached Arabic through the Syriac alchemical/medical translations (Syriac ܐܡܒܝܩܐ ʾambīqā) in the 8th-9th c. Greek -mb- was rendered -nb-, hence the two Arabic spellings anbīq/ambīq that Nourai lists. Nourai's own NOTE ('Some references derive this from Greek ambix') is in fact the unanimous modern view (Klein, Webster's, Etymonline, Wiktionary, Mo'in); the Greek word itself is of unknown, possibly Pre-Greek/substrate or Semitic origin (Beekes). Webster's and Etymonline allow that the word passed 'via Persian' between Greek and Arabic, but even so the Persian stage would be a loan of ambix, not a compound with āb.

ref_check.note: WEB_vol1.txt line 5377 (Webster's New 20th C., s.v. alembic): 'a-lem/bic, n. [L. alambicus; Ar. alanbiq; al, the, and anbiq, Per. ambiq, a still; Gr. ambix, a cup of a still.]' — Persian is only a transit stage; the source is Greek ambix.
Asbaghi — no online copy.

nodes.derivation: NP انبیق anbīq 'still, retort' is a loan of Arabic anbīq/inbīq, taken over with the Arabic alchemical vocabulary in the early Islamic centuries (Mo'in marks it معرّب, ultimately Greek). The chart's arrow Arabic → Persian is right; only the ultimate origin claimed in nodes 5-6 is wrong.

ref_check.note: MON_part1.txt line 17169: 'انبیق: [غ. معر.] (ا.) ظرفی است برای تقطیر مایعات و گرفتن عصاره و عرق' — confirms the word and that Persian took it from Arabic (معرّب), but labels the origin Greek (غ.), against Nourai's Persian âbnîk.

nodes.derivation: Old Spanish/Spanish alambique 'still' is a direct Andalusi-Arabic loan of al-anbīq, article included (as in alcohol, álgebra), with the Arabic -nb- realised as -mb-; Iberian Arabic alchemy (10th-12th c.) is the channel. Klein and Etymonline give exactly this Spanish stage; Wiktionary goes straight from Medieval Latin alembicus to Arabic. Italian lambicco is a parallel loan.

ref_check.note: KLN_1966.txt line 2149 (p.47): 'alembic, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) alambic, fr. OSp. (= Sp.) alambique fr. Arab. al-anbīq, the still, which is formed fr. al-, the, and Gk. ἄμβιξ, cup, cap of a still, alembic, which is of uncertain, possibly Semitic origin. Cp. It. lambicco'.

nodes.derivation: Old French alambic (13th c.) 'still' is taken either from Old Spanish alambique (Klein, Etymonline) or from Medieval Latin alembicus/alambicum, itself the Latinisation of Arabic al-anbīq used in the 12th-c. alchemical translations (Wiktionary). Nourai's NOTE 'could be through Latin alambicum' is the alternative that Wiktionary prefers; both routes exist side by side and are compatible with the chart.

ref_check.note: KLN_1966.txt line 2149: 'fr. OF. (= F.) alambic, fr. OSp. (= Sp.) alambique' — French from Spanish as drawn.

nodes.derivation: Middle English alembic (late 14th c.; aphetic limbeck already mid-14th c., common in the 15th-17th c.) is borrowed from Old French alambic; the -e- of the English form reflects the Medieval Latin spelling alembicus. Meaning 'still' since the alchemists, figurative 'anything that refines' from the 16th c.

ref_check.note: KLN_1966.txt line 2149: 'alembic, n. — ME., fr. OF. (= F.) alambic'; line 21755: 'limbec, n., alembic (archaic). — Aphetic for alembic.'

nodes.derivation: Both are reconstructed rather than attested Pahlavi lemmas. âp-rex = MP *āb-rēz/*ābrēk 'water-pourer' (āb + rēz-, present stem of rēxtan 'to pour', Nourai's ☞Leigh 2 = PIE *leikʷ-); Wiktionary reconstructs 'Middle Persian or Parthian *ābrēk' as the source of Arabic ibrīq, and Jeffery (p.47) already explained the word as Pahlavi āp + rēz 'from an old Iranian root *raek = linquere'. Nourai's spelling with -x may render the Book-Pahlavi ʾplyk/ʾprēk with the older -k. na-âp = MP anāb 'undiluted, pure' (Horn no. 1015: 'nāb rein, ungemischt; aw. an-āp- ohne Wasser; phlv. anāp'), i.e. the privative prefix an-/a- (Nourai's ☞Ne 1) + āb 'water' = 'without water'; NP nāb lost the initial a- by aphaeresis. Neither compound appears as a headword in MacKenzie, hence 'plausible' rather than 'confirmed'.

ref_check.note: FVQ_pages.txt ff-page 64-65 (Jeffery pp.46-47, s.v. ibrīq): 'It would be derived from [āb] water (= Phlv. āp, i.e. OPers. āpi = Av. āp ... ), and [rīz] to pour (= Phlv. rēc from an old Iranian root *raek = linquere) ... It was from the Phlv. form that the word was borrowed into Arabic, the shortening of the ī being regular.'

Bailey, Indo-Scythian Studies (Khotanese Texts VI) is not on disk; the substitute Bailey Dictionary of Khotan Saka (ISS_alt_DKS.txt) was grepped for anāb/nāb/ābrēz without a hit. Horn HRN.txt line 8831 (no. 1015) supplies the same derivation: 'nāb rein, ungemischt. aw. anāp- ohne Wasser; phlv. anāp'.

nodes.derivation: NP ābrīz 'ewer, urn; sink, latrine' is a transparent compound āb + rīz (present stem of rīxtan 'pour'; MP rēz-, with NP ē > ī), Dehkhoda 'دلو' and 'متوضا، مبال'. NP nāb 'pure, undiluted, unalloyed' continues MP anāb (an- privative + āb) with loss of the unstressed initial a- (Horn no. 1015; Wiktionary 'from Middle Persian *anāb'); the sense 'without water' → 'unwatered (wine)' → 'pure' is the same development as Greek ákratos.

ref_check.note: Indo-Scythian Studies not available; substitute DKS text has no nāb/ābrēz entry. Horn HRN.txt line 8831 'nāb rein, ungemischt; aw. anāp- ohne Wasser; phlv. anāp' supports the derivation.

nodes.derivation: Pass-through node for Arabic إِبْرِيق ibrīq (pl. abārīq) 'ewer, water-jug', a pre-Islamic loan from Middle Persian/Parthian *ābrēk/*ābrēz (possibly via Syriac ʾaḇrēqā): attested in the Qur'ān (56:18, abārīq) and in the pre-Islamic poets ʿAdī b. Zayd, ʿAlqama and al-Aʿshā, i.e. borrowed among the Arabs of al-Ḥīra in contact with the Sasanian court; Persian ē was shortened to i and the Iranian z/k rendered by q (Jeffery pp.46-47; Cheung 2017).

ref_check.note: Node carries no refs; FVQ_pages.txt ff-page 64 (Jeffery p.46): 'A ewer, or water jug ... It was early recognized as a Persian loan-word (Siddiqi, 13), and is given by al-Kindī, Risāla, 85; ath-Thaʿālibī, Fiqh, 317; as-Suyūṭī and al-Jawālīqī in their lists of Persian borrowings ... The word occurs in the early poetry ... doubtless an early borrowing among the Arabs who were in contact with the court at al-Ḥīra.'

nodes.derivation: NP ابریق ibrīq/ebrīq 'water-jug, ewer' is a round-trip loan: Persian āb-rēz → Arabic ibrīq → back into Persian in the Arabic form (Mo'in: 'ابریق [معرّب آبریز]'; Jeffery p.47 note 7: 'ibrīq also occurs in Pers. but only as a borrowing from Arabic'; Wiktionary: 'borrowed from Arabic إِبْرِيق'). The Arabic-shaped word (initial i-, -q) co-exists with native ābrīz.

ref_check.note: FVQ_pages.txt ff-page 64-65 (Jeffery p.46-47): 'In modern Persian the word is [ابریق] meaning urn or waterpot ... [ibrīq] also occurs in Pers. but only as a borrowing from Arabic.' Mo'in MON_part1.txt line 6264: 'ابریق: [معر. آبریز] (ا.) ظرف سفالین آب ...' agrees.

nodes.derivation: The name Panjāb/Punjab is a Persian compound پنج panj 'five' (☞Penkwe) + آب āb 'water, river', 'the five rivers' (Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Sutlej); it was coined in the Perso-Islamic period (in use by the Mughal era; earlier writers such as Ibn Baṭṭūṭa use Panj-āb for the Indus confluence) as a calque of the Sanskrit name पञ्चनद Pañcanada (pañca + nada 'river'; Vedic Sapta-sindhu). Sanskrit āp- 'water' is a genuine cognate of Persian āb, but there is no Sanskrit *pañc-āp; the language label 'Sanskrit' is wrong and the word belongs under the Persian branch. The transliteration 'punj' reflects the Anglo-Indian spelling with u.

ref_check.note: AHD_watkins1985.txt: the ap-2 entry (line 282) lists only JULEP; no PUNJAB under ap-2 or in the index. The 1975 AHD main-dictionary entry (not on disk) gives Punjab as Persian panj + āb, which would contradict the Sanskrit label.

nodes.derivation: English Punjab (17th-18th c. Anglo-Indian spelling, earlier Panjab) is taken from Punjabi/Hindustani Pañjāb, itself the Persian پنجاب panjāb 'five waters' used by the Delhi Sultanate and Mughal administration; the u spelling reflects the Hindustani short a heard as [ʌ]. Etymonline: 'from Hindi Panjab, from Persian panj five + ab water'. The English word is correct; only the parent's language label (node 15) is wrong.

ref_check.note: Node carries no refs; Etymonline and Wiktionary used instead.
